claims.text: The superconducting critical temperature of high-entropy alloy superconductors is governed by local lattice distortions induced by atomic-size mismatch.
Local lattice distortions modulate the electron-phonon coupling that supports Cooper pairing.
The proposed initial material is an as-synthesized, disordered, single-solid-solution HEA containing multiple principal elements.
Adjusting alloy composition can systematically vary atomic-size disparity.
Post-synthesis annealing can modify local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions and strain fields can be assessed through X-ray diffraction peak broadening.
Local lattice distortions can be directly visualized using transmission electron microscopy.
Atomic-size mismatch in a disordered alloy produces local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Local lattice distortions increase the density of states at the Fermi level.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling and increased Fermi-level density of states facilitate more effective Cooper pairing.
More effective Cooper pairing produces a higher superconducting critical temperature.
Samples with greater local lattice distortion are predicted to have higher Tc than samples engineered to minimize lattice strain.
Reducing atomic-size disparity through composition optimization is expected to reduce local lattice distortion.
Extended annealing is expected to relieve lattice strain.
A reduced-strain baseline is expected to exhibit lower Tc.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply primarily to HEAs with significant atomic-size mismatch.
Strong electronic correlations or impurity effects may prevent lattice distortion from producing the predicted change in Tc.
The direction of the relationship between lattice distortion and Tc is supported, although its quantitative form is uncertain.
Failure to observe a systematic increase in Tc with increasing measured distortion, or finding similar Tc in markedly low- and high-strain samples, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
